method: 22 independent cold readers, rendered prose only, 8-type taxonomy, severity 1-3

register.quote: Those two award lines name the Greater Akron Chamber, PIC’s own organisation: 4.9 percent of the $85,335,784 awarded.
register.why: This is the first substantive sentence and 'Those two award lines' has no antecedent — I had not been shown any lines yet, so I stopped and scanned backward for something that wasn't there.

register.quote: the Greater Akron Chamber, PIC’s own organisation
register.why: PIC is never expanded anywhere on the page, and the apposition left me unsure whether PIC belongs to the Chamber or the Chamber to PIC.

register.quote: The rest goes straight to six other EDA leads and five state workstreams.
register.why: EDA is never expanded, and 'leads' and 'workstreams' are grant-administration insider words used as if I already knew the program structure.

register.quote: 4.9 percent of the $85,335,784 awarded
register.why: The $85,335,784 figure is used here before the next paragraph defines it as the total of three public awards.

register.quote: All bars on one dollar scale. Read down: reported secured, awarded, reached by a named recipient, then on a line naming the Chamber. The detached bar is match, never part of the total.
register.why: This narrates chart mechanics (bars, reading direction, a detached bar), and the first stage 'reported secured' carries no figure — I only learn it is $106.3 million in the closing line.

register.quote: The other six EDA awards do not pass through it.
register.why: I was told there are three public awards, then suddenly there are seven EDA awards; I had to re-read and infer that one public award splits into seven lines — the three-award structure (EDA, APEX, Ohio Innovation Hub) is never laid out as a trio.

register.quote: EDA is fully assigned and APEX is fully assigned; the entire unassigned balance, $6,165,608, sits in the Ohio Innovation Hub at 80.3 percent, held in two workstreams.
register.why: 'Assigned' is a third name for what the chart calls 'reached by a named recipient' and the table calls 'executed'; I only connected them by doing the subtraction myself.

register.quote: sits in the Ohio Innovation Hub at 80.3 percent
register.why: 80.3 percent of what is never stated — I guessed it means the unassigned share of that one award, but the sentence doesn't say.

register.quote: APEX is fully assigned
register.why: APEX appears here for the first and only time with no expansion or description of what kind of award it is.

register.quote: The dashed outline is the absence of a figure rather than a small one, and nothing on this page estimates what belongs in it.
register.why: Prose about a dashed outline's meaning, and I had to infer from a previous sentence that the absent figure is payment.

register.quote: Of the $3,748,500 startup-support workstream, $225,000 is the nine Synthe6 cohort cash awards and the balance is delivered through the Bounce sub-grant that runs the whole workstream, so publishing “$3,523,500 unassigned” without that sentence manufactures a problem PIC does not have.
register.why: One sentence carries a workstream total, a carve-out, a delivery mechanism, a derived figure, and a meta-claim about publishing ethics — I read it three times.

register.quote: the balance is delivered through the Bounce sub-grant
register.why: 'Synthe6' and 'Bounce' are program/organisation names introduced with zero explanation of what they are.

register.quote: The other gap, $2,642,108 of the $5,992,000 PIC Translational R&D allocation, is genuinely not yet sub-granted.
register.why: I had to add $3,523,500 and $2,642,108 myself to confirm the two gaps compose the $6,165,608 unassigned balance; the page never closes the loop.

register.quote: the largest single line in the assignment test is money assigned to a building that does not exist yet
register.why: 'The assignment test' is used as a named thing but is never defined — I guessed it means the reached-a-named-recipient stage.

register.quote: The rule falls at $1,000,000.
register.why: I first read 'rule' as a regulation; it turns out to mean a horizontal divider line in the table, which only clicked at 'the eleven above the rule' later.

register.quote: The chip on each row says what kind of participation the line records
register.why: 'Chip' is UI-widget vocabulary narrating table furniture rather than the story.

register.quote: An operator at an independent firm reading for a number they could win should read those two rows and not the eleven above the rule.
register.why: The table was declared 'one row per executed award line', but seven sub-grants plus nine cohort awards are here called 'those two rows' — sixteen lines versus two rows is never reconciled.

register.quote: A hollow ring with a centre pip is scheduled and a solid disc is delivered
register.why: Pure legend-narration of mark shapes; I had to hold the encoding in my head to keep reading.

register.quote: Owner attribution is on every row because a target that moves for a state controlling board is not PIC’s slip.
register.why: The phrase 'moves for' (slips because of?) plus the unglossed 'state controlling board' forced a re-read to extract the point that partner delays aren't PIC's fault.

register.quote: The register also carries one standing rule, because without it a promise register creates a reason to stop publishing forward dates: only a date already published is eligible, so publishing a date can never be worse than withholding one.
register.why: The incentive logic is compressed into one colon-chained sentence with a double negative at the end; I re-read it twice before the rule made sense.

register.quote: On 12 December 2025 PolyKinetix was described as selected “5 of 38”.
register.why: '5 of 38' is undecodable — ranked fifth of 38, or one of 5 winners from 38? The section is about denominator confusion, but the phrase itself gives me nothing to hold.

register.quote: The internal board scorecard records eighteen rows, fifteen of which PIC answers for.
register.why: A second, unrelated 'eighteen' arrives immediately after 'eighteen dated commitments'; I paused to check whether these are the same eighteen and the page never distinguishes them.

register.quote: Generated from the shipped files that carry each limitation, so a hand-maintained honesty list cannot go stale here.
register.why: 'Shipped files' (and 'this repository' earlier) is software-process language a general reader of a public page doesn't have — shipped where, by whom?

register.quote: The Tech Hub award is $51,001,413
register.why: 'Tech Hub' appears here for the first time; only by arithmetic did I guess it is the largest of the three public awards mentioned at the top.

register.quote: across the same twelve counties, FY2019 to FY2026, in constant 2025 dollars
register.why: 'The same twelve counties' presumes a geography this page never established — same as what?

register.quote: so this page states the level and the limit and computes no ratio
register.why: 'The limit' has no clear referent — the limit of the comparison? of the instrument? Minor snag at the end of an otherwise careful paragraph.

register.quote: PIC holds $4,149,515 of the $106.3 million it reports securing
register.why: $106.3 million is quantified for the first time in the closing line; the opening chart stage 'reported secured' carried no number, and I had to add $85,335,784 and $20,954,667 myself to see where it comes from.

register.quote: One of those eighteen carries a number that can be missed.
register.why: Cryptic on both axes — which of the eighteen, and does 'missed' mean overlooked or unmet? I stalled on the closing line.

register.quote: The award register behind bands A, B and C.
register.why: The charts above were narrated as 'stages'; the footer suddenly calls them 'bands A, B and C', labels used nowhere else in the prose.

register.quote: Three, in Lowell, Big Rapids and Akron, hold over a third of that record.
register.why: "That record" grammatically points back to institutions reporting, so I couldn't tell if the third is a third of degrees conferred, of institutions, or of reports — I had to guess degrees.

register.quote: Three, in Lowell, Big Rapids and Akron, hold over a third of that record.
register.why: The three institutions are named only by city and never by name; I know Akron but had no idea what university sits in Big Rapids, so the page's most important actors stayed anonymous.

register.quote: It is a floor, not a census, and small enough to list whole: one dot, one institution.
register.why: Three moves in one sentence — an ambiguous "It" (the record? the 147?), an unglossed floor/census metaphor on first use, and a chart mechanic — before any chart had been introduced; I re-read it.

register.quote: sized by every degree and certificate it ever conferred under a polymer heading
register.why: "Under a polymer heading" implies some classification system that is never named or explained — heading of what?

register.quote: Each bar is one institution’s lifetime completions across every polymer program it ever filed, 1991–2023: the twelve largest.
register.why: The colon-appended "the twelve largest" arrives after the definition and date range, so I had to re-read to realize the chart shows only twelve institutions, not all 147.

register.quote: lifetime completions
register.why: The opening paragraphs say "degree or certificate" and "conferred"; here the same thing suddenly becomes "completions" with no bridge, and I paused to confirm they were the same count.

register.quote: the programs page ranks the same record the other way, because the two are different units and neither substitutes for the other
register.why: "Ranks the same record the other way" is abstract, and I had to backtrack to map "the two" onto institutions vs. programs — a page I haven't seen is invoked mid-explanation.

register.quote: every polymer program it ever filed
register.why: "Filed" treats programs as paperwork lodged with the government — plausible given the opening, but the reporting mechanism behind the verb is never explained.

register.quote: Since 1991, 147 American colleges and universities have reported a polymer degree or certificate to the federal government.
register.why: The lede says "since 1991" as if the record runs to the present, but the bar-chart caption later bounds it at 1991–2023; the endpoint is never reconciled.

register.quote: Every company PIC has classified in the fourteen counties, on the chain that turns a molecule into a product and back.
register.why: PIC is the first word of substance and is never expanded or explained anywhere on the page — I read the whole thing without learning what PIC is.

register.quote: in the fourteen counties
register.why: 'the' fourteen counties assumes I already know which region this is; the next block finally says Northeast Ohio, so meaning arrives after the claim.

register.quote: Type what you need to make.
register.why: Abrupt imperative with no signal that this is a search-box instruction — I briefly read it as part of the argument.

register.quote: Classified firms: width is a linear count Expected shape if NEO matched the surrounding megaregion’s mix
register.why: Legend labels run together as prose with no punctuation between them; I re-read to find where one label ends and the next begins.

register.quote: the surrounding megaregion’s mix
register.why: Which megaregion? The term is never named or defined, yet the chart's 'expected shape' baseline depends entirely on it.

register.quote: PIC has classified nothing at all in three of its own counties.
register.why: 'its own counties' implies PIC's footprint differs from the fourteen just mentioned, but the PIC-12 vs NEO-14 distinction is only revealed two paragraphs later.

register.quote: The map is not a count of firms: population would steal that story.
register.why: A map appears without introduction — I was reading about a ribbon — and 'population would steal that story' is cryptic; I had to infer it means raw counts would just mirror population.

register.quote: PIC’s intake form and the vault use compatible value-chain taxonomies
register.why: 'the vault' arrives with a definite article and no definition; I never learn what it is beyond guessing it is PIC's company database.

register.quote: so the companies on record and the projects people want funded can sit on one spine
register.why: 'spine' is a chart-layout term smuggled into the argument; I only understood it after the later 'shared center line' sentence.

register.quote: converters have 12 cataloged companies for every 2026 application
register.why: I first parsed '2026' as a count of applications rather than a year, and 'converters' is an unglossed stage name — two decodings in one clause.

register.quote: cataloged companies
register.why: The same set of companies is called 'classified', 'cataloged', and 'on record' in the span of a few sentences; I paused to check whether these were different sets.

register.quote: Twelve raw-materials companies may be very large plants; 246 converters may be small shops.
register.why: The sentence before used 12 as the converters' ratio; now twelve is the raw-materials company count and 246 appears from nowhere — I stopped and re-read to untangle which 12 was which.

register.quote: (intake is PIC-12, the vault is NEO-14)
register.why: Two coded geography names, never expanded; I inferred NEO-14 is the fourteen counties but PIC-12 is pure guesswork.

register.quote: so the ratio is indicative and is the one place on this site where the two geographies touch
register.why: One sentence carries the footprint mismatch, a hedge ('indicative' of what?), and a site-wide methodological claim; I re-read it.

register.quote: Two different units, drawn on two scales that meet at a shared center line, never one axis, and never a ratio bar.
register.why: A verbless fragment narrating design decisions ('never one axis, and never a ratio bar') that defends the chart rather than telling me what it shows.

register.quote: so both sides sum to more than their totals
register.why: 'sum to more than their totals' reads as self-contradictory on first pass; I re-read to work out that stage counts exceed distinct-company counts because of multi-stage membership.

register.quote: Companies: GAC-PIC vault, 785 classified in NEO-14.
register.why: GAC-PIC is yet another unexpanded acronym stacked onto PIC, though by this point I accepted it as a source label.

register.quote: Applications: pic-innovation-intake-export-2026-07-07.csv, 59 rows.
register.why: A raw internal filename in the prose; honest as provenance but it made me feel I was reading the maker's notes, not a page written for me.

register.quote: Net employment is a legitimate outcome measure, and funders are entitled to score it.
register.why: "Funders" and "a program" appear for the first time in the final two sentences — I had to re-read the ending and reconsider what the whole page was for, since nothing earlier said this was about evaluating a program.

register.quote: The ledger nets them: 111,529 hires, 111,361 separations, +168.
register.why: "The ledger" is unintroduced and these totals cover an unstated window — I only learned it was 2012Q1–2025Q3 in the last paragraph.

register.quote: No: the headcount fell by 719, to 17,725.
register.why: Fell since when, and where? Neither the period nor the region/industry has been named in the prose at this point.

register.quote: That margin is a ledger of flows, and it is not the answer to whether the industry has more jobs.
register.why: The page labels the +168-vs-minus-719 conflict as two different measures ("estimated separately") but never explains how the flows ledger can net positive while the headcount falls by 719.

register.quote: The rise here is almost all on the leaving side
register.why: "The rise" presumes I already know churn rose — that fact is first shown two paragraphs later ("the line settles above where it started"), so I stopped to ask what rise was meant.

register.quote: This pull has no other industry or state to compare against.
register.why: "Pull" is data-analyst insider language for a data extract; a general reader doesn't know a page can have a "pull."

register.quote: Since 2023Q1 more jobs have ended than started every quarter, the second kind of churn, the bad one.
register.why: Stated here as a raw every-quarter fact, but the later chart caption says the streak is "averaged over a year" — I couldn't tell whether the 11-quarter run holds in raw quarters or only in the trailing-year average.

register.quote: The further RIGHT, the more plastics and rubber jobs the county has.
register.why: "Rubber" appears for the first time here — until this caption the page seemed to be about plastics alone, so the industry's scope quietly changed.

register.quote: Over the last four published quarters the cluster moved 9.6% of its jobs in a quarter.
register.why: "The cluster" arrives unintroduced as yet another name for the same thing already called "here," "this pull," "the region," and "the industry."

register.quote: One job in ten here starts and one in ten ends every quarter: about 14 in and 14 out at a 150-person plant.
register.why: One in ten of 150 is 15, not 14 — I stopped to recheck the arithmetic; the 14 actually comes from the 9.6% rate that isn't given until much later. "Here" is also unlocated.

register.quote: about 1,327 events for every one job of that margin
register.why: The sentence carries the window, the event total, the margin, and this ratio; the compressed phrase "one job of that margin" made me re-read to work out what was being divided by what.

register.quote: They are job events, not people: a Summit-to-Stark move counts twice.
register.why: Assumes I know Summit and Stark are counties — they are the first place names on the page and are never identified as counties here.

register.quote: which comes to 434 starts and ends across the four quarters
register.why: The setup says "about 54" and "about 54" per quarter, which multiplies to 432, not 434 — the rounding mismatch trips a reader who checks.

register.quote: Their difference is the net flow, the line.
register.why: "The line" points from the prose at a chart element I haven't seen described, a small jolt of chart mechanics inside a definition.

register.quote: the last four published quarters
register.why: "Published" hints at a data-release lag that is never explained — I briefly wondered why data ends at 2025Q3 and what an unpublished quarter would be.

register.quote: and on the same three-code basis this page counts
register.why: "three-code basis" assumes I know industries are counted by numeric codes, and "basis this page counts" reads like it is missing a word ("counts on"?) — I re-read it to parse the grammar before the colon rescued me.

register.quote: while the region’s fixed-set count of those same industries fell 7.2 percent
register.why: "fixed-set count" is never defined — I guessed it means holding a fixed list of industries constant, but couldn't tell whether it also fixes establishments or geography, and the 7.2 percent hangs on it.

register.quote: The longest bar belongs to concentration, the one measure on this page with no better end at all.
register.why: "concentration" — of what, measured how — arrives with no definition, and "no better end at all" needed a second pass to decode as "neither rising nor falling is good".

register.quote: A bar is the SIZE of this year’s step against how far that measure usually steps
register.why: "this year" is never anchored to a year — the opening paragraph compares 2023 to 2025, a two-year fall, so I couldn't tell whether a "step" is one year or that whole span.

register.quote: so a three-hundredths move in a wage ratio and a $16 million move in contracting land on one axis
register.why: Both figures arrive before I know what the wage ratio compares or what "contracting" is, and I can't tell whether these are this year's actual moves or invented examples.

register.quote: Past 1.0 the move beat the middle of that measure’s own earlier moves, which is what “bigger than usual” means here and which about half of years do.
register.why: Two stacked which-clauses pointing at different antecedents, plus "the middle" standing in for an unnamed median, made me re-read once to get who does what.

register.quote: We have set no target for any of these five, so no tile reports distance from one.
register.why: The display element has been a "bar" for two paragraphs, suddenly becomes a "tile" here, and later a "badge" — I couldn't tell if these are one element or three.

register.quote: Each reports a level, where that level sits in the measure’s own published range, which end of that range is the better one for the region where there is one, a direction against a stated baseline, and the page it came from, where the working is shown in full.
register.why: A five-item list where each item carries its own subordinate clause — I lost the list structure at "where there is one" and had to re-read twice to separate items from qualifiers.

register.quote: The yardstick each bar is measured against is built one way for all five measures.
register.why: The page names concentration, a wage ratio, contracting, employment, degree and spending — six labels for "five measures" — and never lists the five, so I couldn't resolve whether "contracting" and the "spending series" are the same thing.

register.quote: It says nothing about revision, and the difference decides how much weight a fresh figure can carry.
register.why: I had to stop to work out which "difference" was meant (travel-between-years versus revision), and "decides how much weight a fresh figure can carry" is abstract until the next sentence backfills it.

register.quote: A revision measure would say how far the year just published will move once the agencies restate it, and this repository has measured that for exactly three producer-price indexes, the prices factories charge for what they make: 259 reference months of archived earlier releases, a middle revision of 0.15 percent of the level and a largest of 1.42 percent.
register.why: One sentence carries a definition, an inventory claim, an inline gloss, and three statistics — and "259 reference months" plus "0.15 percent of the level" arrived before I understood what a reference month is; I gave up mid-sentence and restarted.

register.quote: Each of these is a live federal series with a known refresh, and one of them is behind the others.
register.why: Which series is behind, and behind in what sense (staler data? missed refresh?), is never said — the sentence raises a flag and drops it.

register.quote: Every figure here is recomputed from the published data of the page it links to, by one script in this folder.
register.why: "this folder" (like the earlier "this repository") addresses me as if I'm browsing a code repo rather than reading a page — a brief where-am-I snag.

register.quote: How much of the fall is the tide.
register.why: As an opening line, "the fall" assumes I already know something fell — the metaphor only resolves once the 7.2 percent lands mid-paragraph.

register.quote: Two independent instruments, publications and federal awards, measured over thirteen years.
register.why: Verbless fragment that never says WHO is being measured — the two universities are never named up front, and I only inferred Case Western and Akron from the NEO-SMART sentence three paragraphs later.

register.quote: 201 coauthored papers, seven classified in polymers, four joint federal awards worth $3.7 million, none starting after 2017 in this window.
register.why: Four figures arrive before I know whose partnership this is; I re-read to decide whether "none starting after 2017" meant the papers or the awards, and "this window" is used as if already defined.

register.quote: An earlier page here said PIC could put the two polymer chairs in the same room
register.why: "PIC" is never expanded anywhere, and "the two polymer chairs" (department chairs? endowed chairs? people?) is insider shorthand — I gave up on knowing what PIC is.

register.quote: The window closes before the largest relevant award exists.
register.why: At this point I still don't know when the window closes — "The series ends in 2024" arrives two paragraphs later, and the start year (2012?) is never stated at all, only recoverable by arithmetic from "thirteen years".

register.quote: That was an unbounded negative resting on data that was never about collaboration
register.why: "Unbounded negative" is a term of art dropped without definition; I slowed to work out it means a limitless claim of absence.

register.quote: Each tick at the base is one paper classified in polymers and plastics, or in biomaterials next to it, a subject classification, not a keyword.
register.why: Three qualifications in one sentence, and "or in biomaterials next to it" is ambiguous — next to it on the chart, or adjacent in the classification scheme? I re-read it.

register.quote: but a reader who knows about it should not have to wonder whether this page does
register.why: The ellipsis "whether this page does" (does what — know about it?) made me back up to resolve the antecedent.

register.quote: They are drawn as individual ticks rather than a proportional band because there are few enough that a band would render as a sliver and read as zero.
register.why: Prose narrating the chart's own rendering choices (ticks, band, sliver) — I understood it, but it is mechanics talk, not the story.

register.quote: Case Western leads the NEO-SMART NSF Engine, awarded 14 July 2026
register.why: "NSF Engine" is a specific federal program name assumed known; a lay reader parses it as an odd metaphor before moving on.

register.quote: the CWRU-led NEO-SMART NSF Engine, July 2026, in which Akron is a core partner
register.why: "Case Western" earlier becomes bare "CWRU" here, and this sentence restates the paragraph-3 NEO-SMART caveat almost verbatim, so I paused to check whether I had missed a difference between the two tellings.

register.quote: The largest joint federal undertaking these two institutions have entered began eighteen months after this window closed.
register.why: "Largest" invites comparison with the $3.7 million just cited, but no figure for NEO-SMART is ever given, so the superlative floats unsupported.

register.quote: so a low count here means not visible at this resolution
register.why: "Means not visible" is grammatically clipped (means "not visible", or means only that it is not visible?) — a small hitch at the end of an otherwise well-motivated sentence.

register.quote: The cluster has members on every link.
register.why: "The cluster" arrives with a definite article as if already introduced — I never learn what cluster this is or whose members these are, and the page never circles back to define it.

register.quote: on the scale in the next chart it peaked at 283 and now reads 93, a fall of 190 against the 183 points it had gained above 100: 104% given back, which is why its bar runs past the line.
register.why: The index scale (January 2019 = 100) is only defined two paragraphs later, so I had to hold 283, 93, 190, 183 and 100 as raw numbers and re-read once the base was finally explained; the sentence also packs the whole subtraction into one breath.

register.quote: What would sharpen this band: one member’s own quoted-price history for a single part, January 2019 to now.
register.why: "This band" names nothing that came before — the gap has been called the line, the cushion, and the scissors, but never a band — and I gave up trying to identify its referent.

register.quote: The desk does not have one, so nothing on this page is a member’s number, and the dollar figures below are the industry average translated into dollars.
register.why: "The desk" is newsroom insider shorthand; no desk, author, or organization has been introduced, so I didn't know who was speaking.

register.quote: the dollar figures below are the industry average translated into dollars
register.why: "Below" points onward, but the only dollar figures ($1.00, $1.14, $1.40) appeared in the paragraph above — I looked for a table further down that never came.

register.quote: That was the converter’s world through the shortage, bottoming 22.5 points under in August 2021.
register.why: "The shortage" arrives with a definite article but no shortage has been mentioned; I had to infer a 2021 resin shortage from context.

register.quote: Resin rose 23.2 points between March and May 2026, nearly a quarter of its 2019 base, the cushion closed to +0.7, its thinnest month since September 2022, and it reopened to +14.3 in July.
register.why: Five claims comma-spliced into one sentence; I re-read to sort which "it" reopened and to keep the 23.2 / +0.7 / +14.3 figures attached to the right things.

register.quote: the cushion closed to +0.7
register.why: The same gap is "the line" in one paragraph, "the cushion" here, "the scissors" in the next section, and "this band" at the end — four names for one concept.

register.quote: And four of the seven prices come in pairs: the federal statistics measure resin twice and finished products twice, once from the industries that make them and once as goods traded on the open market.
register.why: "Seven prices" is the first tally given; only five things had been named, so I stopped to back-count (gas, crude, resin, products, electricity, plus the duplicates) before the sentence made sense.

register.quote: Every number this page later subtracts uses the makers’ pair.
register.why: Cryptic forward reference — what the page will "subtract" and which two series constitute "the makers' pair" only become clear several sections later.

register.quote: Those are cash prices, and the ordering holds after inflation too, which is why it means somebody in this chain ate the spike and somebody banked it.
register.why: Three ideas in one sentence (nominal prices, inflation-robustness, a distributional conclusion) joined by the clunky hinge "which is why it means"; "cash prices" is also unglossed and "this chain" is its first mention.

register.quote: One feedstock breaks the pattern: Ohio industrial electricity peaked this January, not in 2022, and has given back only about a quarter, which is why it sits out of order in the chart below.
register.why: "Feedstock" — and calling electricity one — is only defined in the following sentence, so I briefly backtracked; "sits out of order in the chart below" is also chart mechanics in the prose.

register.quote: West Texas Intermediate crude, the benchmark American oil, crested that June and kept about half of its rise.
register.why: "That June" forces me to fish the year (2022) out of the previous sentence's "August 2022" — a small dangling antecedent.

register.quote: the wave weakened at every link until the last one, where it set.
register.why: "Set" is doing quiet metaphorical work (set like concrete?) and took a beat to parse as "the price rise became permanent".

register.quote: two blades moving apart, the cost of inputs rising as one and the price of the finished part as the other
register.why: Both blades are described as rising, so "moving apart" takes a moment to resolve into rising-at-different-rates rather than moving in opposite directions.

register.quote: the same twelve counties
register.why: "Same" points backward to nothing — this is the first mention of geography, the twelve counties are never named, and the page prose never says what region this is beyond a late mention of the Greater Akron Chamber.

register.quote: In fiscal 2019 the routine flow alone came to $51.6 million, $647,000 more than the whole award.
register.why: The $51.6M is in 2025 dollars but the award it's measured against is as-awarded; the next paragraph restates the award at $51.3 million, which shrinks the gap to roughly $300,000, and the $647,000 figure is never squared with that.

register.quote: the dashed line is the eight-year average
register.why: The headline average is $36.6M "over the seven finished fiscal years," so at this point I couldn't tell which average the dashed line marks; the closing paragraph explains why closed years are used ($34.9M vs $36.6M) but the chart's guide line apparently uses the average the text disavows, and that is never reconciled.

register.quote: The two rubber codes hold 65% of eight years, and the second of them, tire manufacturing, put $20.2 million into FY2022 and recorded nothing at all in FY2023: the region’s total fell $26.6 million between those two years, most of it from that one code, which is why FY2023 is the shortest bar in the year-by-year chart.
